briefing.text: This cohort appears to be hepatocellular carcinoma. The clinical tables seem to hold a hepatitis etiology field (CHRONIC_HEPATITIS_ANY_TYPE: HBV / HCV / NBNC), and sample IDs may carry HB/HC/NBNC prefixes. Confirm both. No table has a ready-made mutational-signature column, but data_mutations.txt has Reference_Allele and Tumor_Seq_Allele2, so you can derive a substitution spectrum yourself: six pyrimidine-collapsed classes (C>A, C>G, C>T, T>A, T>C, T>G), counted per sample and per etiology group. If the cohort and etiology field are confirmed, the hypothesis concerns this study, and under the benchmark convention the label must be True or False, not Not verifiable.
briefing.reason: Stops a wrong 'Not verifiable' answer because no signature column exists, and points to the variables that can actually test the claim.

briefing.text: The cohort is probably very small: about 21 sequenced tumours, roughly 9 HBV, 9-10 HCV and 2 NBNC, each with few exome mutations. Count SNVs per sample and per group first. If many samples have fewer than about 50 SNVs, per-sample signature refitting (deconstructSigs, SigProfiler) overfits. In that case, pool SNVs by etiology group and compare the spectra (6-class, or 96-context if feasible) with chi-square or Fisher tests, and report effect sizes. With so little power, a non-significant p-value is not evidence of no difference. Weigh descriptive differences alongside the test result.
briefing.reason: Sets the statistical approach for tiny groups and prevents misreading low power as a negative result.

briefing.text: 'Somatic mutation pattern' covers more than driver-gene frequencies. It also includes the substitution spectrum. Fisher tests on TP53, CTNNB1, AXIN1 or ARID1A with tiny counts will rarely reach significance, so do not base the conclusion on them alone. Test both gene-level frequencies by etiology group and substitution spectra by etiology group, and reason from the full pattern.
briefing.reason: Defines what the hypothesis requires to be tested so the team does not test too narrow a variable.

briefing.text: Viral etiology may be confounded with alcohol use, age and sex (for example, HCV patients are often older). Cross-tabulate ALCOHOL, AGE and SEX (if present) by hepatitis group. If they are unbalanced, say so in the reasoning and, where n allows, stratify descriptively, because spectral differences might then not be due to the virus.
briefing.reason: Confounding changes how any observed etiology difference should be interpreted.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume the deposited table is a curated gene subset that cannot test the claim, and so both let 'this is the study's own headline finding' decide the label. Neither checked whether the study reported this as a positive finding or as a negative one, for example 'etiology did not change the patterns'. Under the benchmark convention, the reversed form of a finding is labelled False.

Both teams treat 'mutation pattern' as the 6-class substitution spectrum plus gene hits and TMB. Neither tested strand asymmetry, sequence context or indel versus SNV composition, which are the other common meanings of a mutation pattern.

Both teams pool samples as if every sample were independent. Multi-region samples (HC3-1/HC3-2, HC7-1) and synchronous or metachronous nodules (HB11, HC4, HC10, NBNC2) may not be independent primaries.
unused_evidence: The '#seq_samples' header in data_mutations.txt lists 21 sequenced samples. Six clinical samples (HB3, HB4, HC4, HC8, HC12, HC7-2) are not sequenced. If clinical TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS=0 for these was used as real zero burden, the per-group TMB comparison is biased.
Strand column and transcript-level c. notation: these allow a transcribed versus untranscribed strand analysis of substitutions. Neither team used them.

LIVER_FIBROSIS, EDMONDSON_GRADE and MULTIPLE_NODULES: fibrosis stage and nodule status could confound an etiology comparison. Team A checked only age, sex and alcohol, and Team B reported no confounder check.
Indels (10 frameshift, 1 inframe deletion) were left out of the spectrum. Indel share by etiology is also a mutation pattern.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named the same weakest point: no test in the data supports the claim, so the label rests on recognising the study's finding. Neither team resolved this. They only reported it, and neither checked the direction of the reported finding.
Team B named the double counting of multi-region samples but did not rerun any test with one sample per patient.
Team A named confounding by age and alcohol but did not stratify, even descriptively (for example, spectra among non-drinkers only).
second_readings: 'Mutation patterns' could mean the substitution spectrum or signature, the set of mutated driver genes, mutation burden, or strand or context patterns. These readings could point to different labels.
'Hepatitis B or C virus' could mean comparing HBV against HCV, or comparing viral against non-viral (NBNC) tumours. With only 2 NBNC tumours, the second reading is close to untestable.
'Influences' is causal. A cohort with confounded age and alcohol supports at most an association.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed True label moderately. Neither team's data test supports it, and both rest on recognising the claim as the study's own finding without checking that the study stated it in this direction rather than reversed. The questions target that point, the sample handling (unsequenced and multi-region samples) and the unused readings of 'pattern'.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your label rests on study identity rather than a test. What check did you make that the finding you attribute to the study is stated as etiology influencing mutation patterns, and not as etiology not influencing them? Would the reversed form change your label under the benchmark convention?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Tabulate LIVER_FIBROSIS and EDMONDSON_GRADE by HBV/HCV, and recompute the pooled 6-class spectrum among non-drinkers only. Does any HBV-HCV spectral difference keep its direction, and does that change how you weigh the descriptive evidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Using the Strand column and the transcript c. notation, count substitutions on the transcribed versus untranscribed strand per etiology group, and compare indel share between HBV and HCV. Does either reading of 'pattern' disagree with your spectrum-based conclusion?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: The '#seq_samples' header lists 21 sequenced samples, and HB3, HB4, HC4, HC8, HC12 and HC7-2 are not among them. Did your TMB Mann-Whitney include these samples' clinical TMB values as zeros? If you restrict it to sequenced samples with one sample per patient, does the result change?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Rerun the gene-by-etiology crosstab with one sample per patient, and check whether the HCV-only genes you cite (ATM, USP25) come only from the multi-region samples HC3-1/HC3-2 or HC7-1. Do the gene-level splits you cite as support survive?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You decided from 'the study's headline result'. What check did you make that the study reported etiology as influencing mutation patterns rather than the reversed statement? Would your label change if the hypothesis were the reversed form?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Cross-tabulate ALCOHOL, AGE, LIVER_FIBROSIS and nodule status by etiology; you reported no confounder check. Does any imbalance change whether the differences you observed can be attributed to virus type?

In cancer genomics, how is a difference in 'somatic mutation pattern' between patient groups usually defined and tested: the substitution spectrum, transcriptional strand bias, the trinucleotide context, or driver gene frequencies? Which test is standard when each group has very few mutations?
questions.why: Both teams read 'mutation pattern' only as the 6-class spectrum and gene hits. If strand asymmetry or context is the usual meaning, they may have weighed the wrong kind of evidence.

questions.question: In whole-genome sequencing studies of hepatocellular carcinoma, what differences in somatic substitution patterns (for example, strand bias or specific substitution classes) have been reported between HBV-related and HCV-related tumours?
questions.why: Both teams decided from recalled study findings without checking their direction. Established biology on HBV versus HCV patterns would show whether the claim matches the reported direction or its reverse.

findings.question: In cancer genomics, how is a difference in 'somatic mutation pattern' between patient groups usually defined and tested: the substitution spectrum, transcriptional strand bias, the trinucleotide context, or driver gene frequencies? Which test is standard when each group has very few mutations?
findings.answer: The web did not settle this: the search gateway returned HTTP 403/502 on every call. From domain knowledge, not checked: 'mutation pattern' usually means the substitution spectrum (6 pyrimidine-collapsed classes, often extended to 96 trinucleotide contexts and signatures). Transcriptional strand bias is a further feature of the pattern. Driver gene frequency is treated as a separate question. With few mutations per group, the usual test is a chi-square or Fisher exact test (or Monte Carlo) on pooled class counts, plus a binomial test of transcribed vs untranscribed counts for strand bias.

findings.question: In whole-genome sequencing studies of hepatocellular carcinoma, what differences in somatic substitution patterns (for example, strand bias or specific substitution classes) have been reported between HBV-related and HCV-related tumours?
findings.answer: The web did not settle this: the gateway failed, and PubMed 22634756 was blocked for this lab. Recalled but not checked: early Japanese whole-genome HCC studies (about 27 HBV/HCV tumours) reported that etiological background influences somatic substitution patterns and rates. They also noted transcriptional strand bias of T>C/A>G substitutions in liver cancer. I could not confirm which direction the HBV-vs-HCV difference ran. As I recall it, the reported conclusion supports 'etiology influences mutation patterns', not its reverse.
